first_impression.reaction: Jumped to the FAQ first, as I always do. The answers were short and didn't try to sell me anything, so I went back up and read the comparison table and the tier checklist. The intro is a bit flowery ('quiet workhorse') but it promises a comparison and a list of questions to ask before paying, and that's what I came for. I did notice straight away that it names no actual tools. For a search like 'wedding rsvp website' I half expected a shortlist. Still, a neutral checklist I can run on my own shortlist is arguably more useful than someone else's ranking, especially one that might be paid placement.

journey.quote: Yes, on a no-cost tier. Check guest and event limits, custom questions, export, branding and ads before you commit.
journey.reaction: Straight answer, and it doesn't push me to pay. Good start. That's why I kept reading.

journey.quote: A wedding RSVP website is the quiet workhorse of a destination wedding.
journey.reaction: Fluff. Doesn't put me off, but it's a sentence I skip.

journey.section: The five kinds of wedding RSVP website compared
journey.quote: There is no single right tool, only the right kind for your guest list, judged on what a destination weekend asks of it.
journey.reaction: Fair enough. No 'best RSVP site of 2026' nonsense. The table with a trade-off column for every option is the most useful thing on the page.

journey.quote: Wonderland Studio, our planning app for seating charts and RSVPs, sits in this group.
journey.reaction: At least they say it's theirs and don't call it the best. I'd still want to know whether it costs anything and whether it passes their own checklist.

journey.section: What changes between paid tiers and those at no cost
journey.quote: Will your guests see advertising on the page?
journey.reaction: This is the kind of catch I'd want flagged, and they flagged it. The whole list is a decent due-diligence checklist. I'd paste it into my spreadsheet.

journey.quote: Your Wedded Advisor plans venue, travel, vendors and payments with you, so these answers have somewhere useful to go.
journey.reaction: Hang on, 'your' Wedded Advisor? I don't have one. That's a sales line slipped into a how-to, and it assumes I've already signed up. Also, 'payments'. Whose payments, and does anyone take a cut on the way through? The page doesn't say.

journey.section: Guest privacy and who can see the site
journey.quote: As general information as at November 2026, and not legal advice: personal information includes information or an opinion that could identify an individual, depending on whether that person is identifiable in the circumstances.
journey.reaction: Dated, sourced to the OAIC, and honest about the limits. That's the sort of thing I'd go and check on the government site, and I expect it would hold up.

journey.section: Guest privacy and who can see the site
journey.quote: Weighing several events, room blocks and a guest list across time zones? Talk to our Wedded Concierge team about the weekend you have in mind.
journey.reaction: Second sales push before I've even reached the QR section. Not offensive, but it's a CTA in the middle of the information I came for.

journey.section: QR code RSVPs and when to print the link too
journey.quote: The Australian Cyber Security Centre advises going directly to official websites rather than following links in messages.
journey.reaction: A real source and practical advice (print the address beside the code). Fine.

journey.section: How to set up your RSVP website step by step
journey.quote: Reply as a couple with a child and as a guest who declines one event, and check each answer lands where you expect.
journey.reaction: Good. A test case I can actually run. More of this, less mood.

journey.section: Plan the weekend, not just the replies
journey.quote: one Wedded Advisor, start to finish, as a single point of contact.
journey.reaction: OK, but what does that cost and how are they paid? Nothing here on the fee model. I wouldn't expect it in an RSVP article, but it's the first thing I'd ask before clicking.

unanswered_questions: Does Wonderland Studio cost anything, and does it have a no-cost tier? The page tells me to check every tool for limits, branding and ads, but doesn't run its own checklist on its own app.
What does a Wedded Advisor cost, and how is the fee charged?
The advisor handles 'payments': do you take a commission or mark-up from venues or suppliers?
Which actual RSVP tools did you look at to build this comparison? (I understand if you won't name them, but then I'll be checking Reddit for that.)

turn_offs_found.quote: Your Wedded Advisor plans venue, travel, vendors and payments with you, so these answers have somewhere useful to go.
turn_offs_found.why: Assumes I'm already a client and drops a sales pitch into a practical section. Reads as the catch showing.

turn_offs_found.quote: It is a graceful shortcut, with one caution.
turn_offs_found.why: Emotional wording where a plain statement would do. Minor.

turn_offs_found.quote: Weighing several events, room blocks and a guest list across time zones? Talk to our Wedded Concierge team about the weekend you have in mind.
turn_offs_found.why: CTA mid-article, before the practical content is finished. There are three Concierge CTAs on one page about RSVP forms.

would_share_with: My fiancee, for the tier checklist and the step-by-step test
Whoever ends up building the RSVP form on our side

cta_reaction.quote: Start the conversation with our Wedded Concierge team.
cta_reaction.why: The article earned some trust on RSVP tools, but it gives me nothing on what the advisor service costs or how it's paid. I enquire only once my main questions are answered on the page, and the fee question isn't. I'd bookmark the checklist and go and look for a pricing or FAQ page elsewhere on the site.

top_3_changes: Make the advisor line conditional so it doesn't assume I'm a client. Old: "Your Wedded Advisor plans venue, travel, vendors and payments with you, so these answers have somewhere useful to go." New: "If you work with a Wedded Advisor, they plan venue, travel, vendors and payments with you, so these answers have somewhere useful to go."

Have the brand hold its own app to the same standard it sets for everyone else (no new facts, just the instruction). Old: "It belongs to the fourth kind in the table above, for couples who would like their replies and their seating chart in the same place." New: "It belongs to the fourth kind in the table above, for couples who would like their replies and their seating chart in the same place. Run the same tier questions on it as you would on any tool on your shortlist."

Cut the mid-article CTA so the practical content runs uninterrupted, leaving the two later Concierge links. Old: "Weighing several events, room blocks and a guest list across time zones? Talk to our [Wedded Concierge](/wonderland-concierge?utm_source=blog&utm_medium=content&utm_campaign=wedding-rsvp-website&utm_content=primary) team about the weekend you have in mind." New: "" (delete the paragraph). Lesser alternative if CRO needs it: keep it but move it below the QR code section.

checks.check: Every journey point, turn-off and CTA reaction quotes an exact sentence from 05-draft.md
Stayed in character as Daniel (sceptic): FAQ first, fee and commission focus, plain voice
No invented brand facts; fee, commission, Studio pricing and platform names left as unanswered questions
Suggested edits are exact old/new strings within brand limits (no platforms named, no fees, commissions, sourcing or vetting claims added)
HTML comments and fact markers treated as invisible
Did not invent problems; positives recorded where the page earned them
top_3_changes has at most 3 items; scores within 1 to 5

open_questions.question: The sceptic's main barrier to enquiring is the absent fee and commission model, which the brand has deliberately deferred from this post. Treat as out of scope for this draft, or flag to Nic for a link to a fee or FAQ page if one exists?
Is Wonderland Studio free or paid? The sceptic expects the brand to answer its own tier checklist for its own app, but nothing can be added without a source and Nic's sign-off.

assumptions: Persona card is provisional (not CRM-calibrated), so reactions reflect the assumed profile.
Read as a groom comparing planners who arrived from a generic tool search, so relevance is moderate rather than high.
Absence of platform names and fee details is a deliberate brand decision for this post and was not scored as a defect in itself.
